prodigy.method: PRODIGY (PROtein binDIng enerGY prediction), Vangone & Bonvin eLife 2015;4:e07454 (DOI 10.7554/eLife.07454) IC-NIS model; web server Xue et al., Bioinformatics 2016;32(23):3676-3678 (DOI 10.1093/bioinformatics/btw514). Contacts-based multiple linear regression predicting dG of protein-PROTEIN complexes from 4 interfacial-contact counts + 2 non-interacting-surface composition percentages. Retrieved this session from: (a) Europe PMC full-text XML of the eLife paper (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4523921/fullTextXML), (b) the maintained reference source github.com/haddocking/prodigy cloned at commit 6c459597af54329b65b039ad2458c0976e09c43c, (c) the authors' original 2016 source github.com/JoaoRodrigues/binding_affinity commit 3b535611efa14399021848e359dc532a8df34270, (d) the official method page https://wenmr.science.uu.nl/prodigy/method (raw HTML, not a summarizer). END-TO-END VERIFIED: pip-installed prodigy-prot run on the shipped example 3BZD.pdb reproduced the shipped reference output exactly (51 ICs; CC=4, CP=7, CA=6, PP=7, AP=15, AA=12; %NIS_apolar=29.48, %NIS_charged=29.48; dG = -9.4 kcal/mol, Kd = 1.3e-07 M at 25 C), and hand-evaluating the coefficients below on those same counts gives -9.374, matching.
prodigy.equation:
AUTHORITATIVE SIGNED FORM (this is what the code and the web server compute; dG is negative for a binder):

dG_predicted [kcal/mol] = -0.09459 * IC_charged/charged
                          -0.10007 * IC_charged/apolar
                          +0.19577 * IC_polar/polar
                          -0.22671 * IC_polar/apolar
                          +0.18681 * %NIS_apolar
                          +0.13810 * %NIS_charged
                          -15.9433

Verbatim from src/prodigy_prot/modules/models.py, function IC_NIS(ic_cc, ic_ca, ic_pp, ic_pa, p_nis_a, p_nis_c), lines 19-27:
    return (
        -0.09459 * ic_cc
        + -0.10007 * ic_ca
        + 0.19577 * ic_pp
        + -0.22671 * ic_pa
        + 0.18681 * p_nis_a
        + 0.13810 * p_nis_c
        + -15.9433
    )
Byte-identical coefficients appear in the authors' original repo lib/models.py lines 20-21.

*** SIGN-CONVENTION WARNING — THIS IS THE TRAP THAT PRODUCED THE EARLIER MUTUALLY SIGN-FLIPPED RETRIEVALS ***
The PUBLISHED eLife Equation 2 is printed as the EXACT NEGATION of the above:
  dG_calc = 0.09459 ICs_charged/charged + 0.10007 ICs_charged_apolar - 0.19577 ICs_polar/polar + 0.22671 ICs_polar/apolar - 0.18681 %NIS_apolar - 0.13810 %NIS_charged + 15.9433
(transcribed from the <disp-formula> labelled "(2)" in the Europe PMC XML). This is NOT a typo: the paper regresses against the ABSOLUTE VALUE of dG — Figure 1/Figure 2 captions state "binding affinities are reported as absolute values". Published Eq. 2 therefore returns |dG| (positive, e.g. +9.374 for 3BZD); the code returns signed dG (-9.374). Both are the same model. Implement the signed form; if you transcribe Eq. 2 as-is you get the right magnitude with the wrong sign.

TWO FURTHER PUBLISHED-SOURCE CORRUPTIONS FOUND, do not copy either:
1. eLife Table 3, Model 6 lists slightly DIFFERENT weights than Eq. 2 (a different fit run, differing in the 4th decimal): CC 0.09420, C/A 0.10038, P/P -0.19522, P/A 0.22609, %NIS_apolar -0.18786, %NIS_charged -0.13872, intercept 15.9433. USE Eq. 2 / the code values, not Table 3 — the code values are what reproduce the published example.
2. The official method page https://wenmr.science.uu.nl/prodigy/method prints its Equation 1 in the correct signed form but with the %NIS_charged coefficient mistyped as "+0.3810" (a dropped "1"). Correct value is 0.13810.

Kd CONVERSION (src/prodigy_prot/modules/utils.py, dg_to_kd):
    Kd = exp( dG / (R * T) ),  R = 0.0019858775 kcal K^-1 mol^-1,  T = temp_Celsius + 273.15
Default temperature 25.0 C (298.15 K). Web page states this as "dG = RT ln Kd".

SEPARATE, NOT THE MAIN MODEL — the NIS-only model (Kastritis et al. 2014) also shipped in models.py:
    dG = 0.0856851248873 * %NIS_polar - 0.0685254498746 * %NIS_charged + 0.0261591389985 * n_interface_atoms + 3.0124939659498
This one is NOT used by the prodigy CLI; IC_NIS is.

prodigy.definitions:
=== 1. CONTACT DEFINITION AND DISTANCE CUTOFF ===
CUTOFF = 5.5 Angstrom. Confirmed in three places: (a) eLife Results: "we end up with a reliable dataset of 81 structures (a 'cleaned' dataset) showing an increased correlation of R_ICs = -0.59 (p<0.0001) at the re-optimized distance threshold of 5.5 A to define a contact... All further results will therefore refer to the 5.5 A cut-off to define ICs."; (b) code default d_cutoff=5.5 in calculate_ic() (prodigy.py L16) and predict(distance_cutoff=5.5) (L150), CLI --distance-cutoff default=5.5 (cli.py L31); (c) wenmr method page: "Two residues are defined in contact if any of their heavy atom is within a distance of 5.5 A."

WHICH ATOMS ARE COUNTED: any pair of atoms, residue-level. eLife Methods: "Two residues are considered in contact if a pair of (any) atoms belonging to two residues is closer than a defined cut-off distance." Implementation: Bio.PDB.NeighborSearch(all atoms).search_all(radius=5.5, level='R') — i.e. residue-level pairs, each pair counted ONCE regardless of how many atom pairs are within 5.5 A. So IC counts are residue-pair counts, not atom-pair counts.
HYDROGENS ARE STRIPPED before the search (parsers.py validate_structure, clean=True, removes every atom with element == 'H'), so it is effectively heavy-atom only, consistent with the web page wording.
Only inter-molecular pairs are kept: with a --selection, pairs must come from residues in two DIFFERENT selection groups; without one, pairs must come from different chains (prodigy.py L27-40).
ICs in the eLife paper were originally computed with the COCOMAPS web tool (Vangone et al., 2011); the shipped code reimplements this.

STRUCTURE PREPROCESSING (parsers.py validate_structure), all of it affects the counts:
 - waters and HETATM residues removed (res.id[0][0] in {'W','H'});
 - a non-standard amino acid that is not caught by that filter raises ValueError("Unsupported non-standard amino acid found") — the code REFUSES to run;
 - altloc: only the selected_child of each disordered atom is kept;
 - any residue with a non-blank insertion code is DELETED outright (L83-86);
 - chain gaps only produce a warning.

=== 2. RESIDUE-TO-CLASS ASSIGNMENT — CRITICAL: THE CODE USES *TWO DIFFERENT* CLASSIFICATIONS, AND NEITHER PUBLISHED SOURCE SAYS SO ===

(2a) For the IC (contact) bins — dict aa_character_ic, aa_properties.py L6-27, byte-identical in both repos:
  APOLAR (A): ALA, CYS, GLY, PHE, ILE, MET, LEU, PRO, TRP, VAL, TYR   -> A,C,G,F,I,M,L,P,W,V,Y  (11)
  POLAR  (P): ASN, GLN, SER, THR                                       -> N,Q,S,T               (4)
  CHARGED(C): GLU, ASP, HIS, LYS, ARG                                  -> E,D,H,K,R             (5)
  (the source carries a literal "# ?" comment next to CYS: 'A')

(2b) For the NIS percentages — dict aa_character_protorp, aa_properties.py L29-50:
  APOLAR : ALA, GLY, PHE, ILE, MET, LEU, PRO, VAL       -> A,G,F,I,M,L,P,V   (8)
  POLAR  : CYS, HIS, ASN, GLN, SER, THR, TRP, TYR       -> C,H,N,Q,S,T,W,Y   (8)
  CHARGED: GLU, ASP, LYS, ARG                           -> E,D,K,R           (4)

(2c) What the eLife paper actually prints (Methods, verbatim): "Residues were classified based on their physico-chemical properties as follow: polar: C, H, N, Q, S, T, Y, W apolar: A, F, G, I, V, M, P charged: E, D, K, R."
  -> This equals (2b) EXCEPT the paper's apolar list omits L (LEU) entirely — only 19 of 20 residues are listed. That is a printing error in the paper; the code assigns LEU to apolar.
  -> The paper gives ONE list and does not disclose that a different list (2a) is used for the IC bins.

(2d) What the official web method page prints (verbatim): "polar: C, H, N, Q, S, T, W apolar: A, F, G, I, L, V, M, P, Y charged: E, D, K, R" — presented as the classification for the ICs. This is a THIRD variant: it disagrees with the code's IC dict (2a) on C, H and W (page: polar; code: C->apolar, H->charged, W->apolar) and disagrees with the paper (2c) on Y.
  -> RESOLUTION: use (2a) for ICs and (2b) for NIS. Those are what the executable produces, and they are the pair that reproduces the shipped 3BZD reference output. Do NOT implement the paper's or the web page's single list for the ICs.

=== 3. NIS AND RELATIVE SOLVENT ACCESSIBILITY ===
Operational definition, from freesasa_tools.execute_freesasa_api() + prodigy.analyse_nis():
 - SASA is computed ONCE, on the ASSEMBLED COMPLEX (the whole Bio.PDB Model), not on separated components. Note: parse_structure() calls validate_structure() with no chain selection, so ALL chains present in the file are in the SASA calculation even if --selection names only two of them.
 - Engine: the freesasa Python API, calc(struct) with library defaults -> Lee-Richards algorithm, probe radius 1.4 A, 20 slices (verified by querying freesasa.Parameters() in this session). The eLife paper used NACCESS (Hubbard & Thornton 1993) with "a 1.4 A radius sphere"; the distributed code uses freesasa configured with a NACCESS-equivalent atom-radius classifier shipped at src/prodigy_prot/data/naccess.config (C_ALI 1.87, C_CAR 1.76, C_NUC 1.80, N_AMN 1.50, N_AMD 1.65, N_NUC 1.60, O 1.40, S 1.85, SE 1.80, P 1.90).
 - Per-residue absolute ASA = sum of its atoms' areas. RSA = residue_ASA / rel_asa['total'][resname], where rel_asa['total'] is the NACCESS ALA-X-ALA extended-peptide reference set hard-coded in aa_properties.py L81-103: ALA 107.95, CYS 134.28, ASP 140.39, GLU 172.25, PHE 199.48, GLY 80.10, HIS 182.88, ILE 175.12, LYS 200.81, LEU 178.63, MET 194.15, ASN 143.94, PRO 136.13, GLN 178.50, ARG 238.76, SER 116.50, THR 139.27, VAL 151.44, TRP 249.36, TYR 212.76. (Backbone-only and sidechain-only reference tables are also present but unused by the IC-NIS path.) RSA is therefore a FRACTION in [0,~1], not a percentage.
 - THRESHOLD: acc_threshold = 0.05, i.e. RSA >= 5%. A residue is counted as an NIS residue iff its RSA in the COMPLEX is >= 0.05. Source: prodigy.py analyse_nis(sasa_dict, acc_threshold=0.05) L86 and predict(acc_threshold=0.05) L151; CLI --acc-threshold default=0.05 (cli.py L37); identical default in the authors' 2016 repo predict_IC.py L75/L108 and predict_NIS.py L29/L76. The eLife paper does NOT state this threshold — it defers to Kastritis et al. 2014 (J Mol Biol 426:2632-2652, doi 10.1016/j.jmb.2014.04.017), which is paywalled and was NOT retrieved this session. The 0.05 value is taken from code, not from that paper.
 - The "non-interacting" part is IMPLICIT, not an explicit exclusion: because SASA is computed on the assembled complex, true interface residues are buried and mostly fall below the 5% cutoff and thus drop out on their own. There is no separate interface-residue subtraction step.
 - PERCENTAGES: counts are bucketed by aa_character_protorp into [apolar, charged, polar] (index map A->0, C->1, P->2) and converted as 100.0 * count_class / total_NIS_residue_count. So %NIS_x are percentages OF NIS RESIDUE COUNTS (they sum to 100), NOT percentages of surface area. They are fed to the equation on the 0-100 scale.
 - Return order is (apolar, charged, polar); predict() assigns nis_a, nis_c, nis_p and passes only nis_a and nis_c to IC_NIS.

=== 4. WORKED VERIFICATION (do not skip when porting) ===
Example 3BZD.pdb shipped with the repo: ICs total 51; CC=4, CP=7, CA=6, PP=7, AP=15, AA=12; %NIS_apolar=29.48, %NIS_charged=29.48.
 -0.09459*4 -0.10007*6 +0.19577*7 -0.22671*15 +0.18681*29.48 +0.13810*29.48 -15.9433
 = -0.37836 -0.60042 +1.37039 -3.40065 +5.50716 +4.07119 -15.9433 = -9.374 kcal/mol
Shipped reference file examples/3BZD.ic_model: "-9.373". Freshly installed prodigy-prot run in this session: "-9.4" / Kd 1.3e-07 M. All three agree. Note how the two NIS terms contribute +9.58 kcal/mol against a -15.94 intercept — the NIS block dominates the arithmetic; the interface contacts move the result by only about -3.0 kcal/mol here.
prodigy.reported_accuracy: Pearson r = 0.73 (reported as R = -0.73 in the paper because it correlates predictions against |dG|; p < 0.0001), RMSE = 1.89 kcal/mol. This is on the TRAINING data (the model was fit on the same 81 complexes), mitigated by 4-fold cross-validation repeated 10 times (eLife Methods: "partitioning the dataset into four complementary subsets, training on the 75% of the data and validating on the other 25%... repeated 10 times"). Stratified by conformational change (wenmr method page, raw text): rigid cases i_RMSD <= 1.0 A -> r = 0.75, RMSE = 1.88 kcal/mol; flexible cases i_RMSD > 1.0 A -> r = 0.73, RMSE = 1.89 kcal/mol. eLife Table 3 Model 6 column: R = -0.73, p < 0.0001, RMSE = 1.89. Competing models in the same table for context: ICs_total alone R = -0.59 / RMSE 2.25; BSA_total R = -0.46 / RMSE 2.46. The Bioinformatics 2016 server paper repeats 0.73 and 1.89 and adds no new validation set. NO independent, blind, or held-out test set beyond the 4-fold CV was reported in either paper.
prodigy.accuracy_dataset: The 'cleaned' subset of 81 protein-protein complexes derived from the structure-based protein-protein binding affinity benchmark of Kastritis, Moal, Hwang, Weng, Bates, Bonvin & Janin, Protein Science 2011;20:482-491 (doi 10.1002/pro.580). Derivation chain, verbatim from eLife Methods: the benchmark's 144 non-redundant complexes minus 3 cases with non-unique dG (1NSN, 1UUG, 1IQD) minus 19 cases with gaps/unresolved fragments at the interface (gap = missing segment longer than two residues) = 122 complexes; then removing entries measured by inhibition assay (17) and fluorescence spectrophotometry (19) plus the sparse methods (potentiometry, radioligand, reduction assay, sedimentation) = 81 complexes measured by stopped-flow, SPR, spectroscopy or ITC. APPLICABILITY DOMAIN OF THAT SET, all figures retrieved verbatim from eLife Methods: bound crystal structures only; complex types antibody/antigen 10, enzyme/inhibitor 34, enzyme/substrate 9, enzyme/regulatory subunit 7, G-protein 15, membrane receptor 7, miscellaneous 26, non-cognate 9; dG range -4.3 to -18.6 kcal/mol; interface BSA range 808 to 3370 Angstrom^2; unbound-vs-bound interface RMSD 0.17 to 4.90 A.

blockers: NOT A BLOCKER BUT MUST BE STATED FIRST — PEPTIDE APPLICABILITY. PRODIGY is for protein-PROTEIN complexes and the authors NEVER validated it on peptides. I searched the complete eLife full text retrieved from Europe PMC for 'peptid' (case-insensitive): ZERO occurrences. A fetch of the Bioinformatics 2016 server paper searching for 'peptide', 'protein-peptide', 'oligopeptide', 'short chains' also returned no mentions. The title, abstract, method page and both papers say 'protein-protein complexes' throughout. Applying it to 26-47mers is OUTSIDE its stated applicability, on retrieved evidence: (i) the training set is 81 crystal structures of globular protein-protein complexes with interface BSA 808-3370 A^2 — a 26-47mer will typically bury far less; (ii) the model was fit against dG in -4.3 to -18.6 kcal/mol; (iii) mechanistically, the %NIS terms are computed over the whole assembled complex, so for a small peptide against a large protein the NIS composition is essentially that of the protein partner alone and the peptide barely perturbs it — the prediction collapses toward a near-constant (intercept + partner's NIS terms) modulated only by the handful of IC counts, exactly the regime the regression was never fit in. This is my structural analysis of the retrieved code, flagged as inference, not a published statement. The authors published no applicability statement covering peptides either way; the only limitation they state (Bioinformatics 2016, verbatim) is 'While our method performs well on average, errors in particular cases may be expected; for instance, some natural ultra-high-affinity complexes have average or below-average buried surface area, and our method may underestimate their affinity.' Recommendation: if PRODIGY is used on 26-47mers in this project, report it as an out-of-domain extrapolation with no published validation, not as a calibrated dG.

SIGN CONVENTION — the single highest-risk item, and demonstrably the cause of the earlier mutually sign-flipped retrievals. eLife Equation 2 as printed is the EXACT NEGATION of the implemented equation because the paper regresses on |dG| ('binding affinities are reported as absolute values', Figure 1/2 captions). Implement the signed form from models.py: -0.09459/-0.10007/+0.19577/-0.22671/+0.18681/+0.13810/-15.9433. Validate any port against the shipped 3BZD example (-9.373); if you get +9.37 you copied Eq. 2 verbatim.

THREE PUBLISHED SOURCES DISAGREE ON THE RESIDUE CLASSIFICATION FOR THE IC BINS, and the code's IC classification is NOT documented anywhere in the literature. The code silently uses two different dicts: aa_character_ic for contacts (C->apolar, H->charged, W->apolar, Y->apolar; polar is only N,Q,S,T) and aa_character_protorp for NIS (the PROTORP-style list the paper prints). The eLife paper prints only the second list, and omits LEU from its apolar list (19 of 20 residues). The official web method page prints a third variant for the ICs (C, H, W as polar; Y as apolar). Anyone implementing from either published list will get different IC bin counts and a different dG. Only the code reproduces the reference output. This is retrieved and resolved, but it is a real hazard for anyone re-deriving PRODIGY from the papers.

eLife TABLE 3 MODEL 6 DISAGREES WITH EQUATION 2 IN THE 4th DECIMAL (Table 3: 0.09420 / 0.10038 / -0.19522 / 0.22609 / -0.18786 / -0.13872; Eq. 2 and the code: 0.09459 / 0.10007 / -0.19577 / 0.22671 / -0.18681 / -0.13810; shared intercept 15.9433). Use the Eq.2/code values — they are the ones that reproduce the distributed reference output. Table 3 appears to be a slightly different fit run.

THE OFFICIAL WEB METHOD PAGE MISPRINTS %NIS_charged AS 0.3810 (dropped '1'; correct 0.13810). A 2.76x error on a term worth ~+4 kcal/mol in a typical case. Do not transcribe the coefficients from that page.

MINOR / NOT RETRIEVED: the 5% relative-solvent-accessibility threshold for selecting NIS residues is NOT stated in the eLife paper — the paper defers to Kastritis, Rodrigues, Folkers, Boelens & Bonvin, J Mol Biol 2014;426:2632-2652 (doi 10.1016/j.jmb.2014.04.017), which is paywalled (Europe PMC confirms isOpenAccess=N, no PMCID) and was NOT retrieved this session. The value acc_threshold=0.05 is taken from the executable code, where it is the default in four separate places across two independent repositories, so it is operationally certain; but the primary-literature justification for 5% specifically is NOT RETRIEVED.

MINOR IMPLEMENTATION CAVEAT, from reading the code: SASA (and hence NIS) is computed over EVERY chain present in the input file, because parse_structure() calls validate_structure() without passing the user's --selection. If a structure has three chains and you predict only for A-B, chain C still contributes to %NIS_apolar and %NIS_charged. Strip unwanted chains from the input file if that is not what you want.

MINOR: the code hard-refuses non-standard amino acids (raises ValueError) and silently DELETES any residue carrying a PDB insertion code. For engineered or modified peptides this will either crash or quietly change the interface. Check inputs.

B. fnat — 5.0 Å heavy-atom cutoff, residue-residue contact. See `definitions`.

C. iRMSD / LRMSD — see `definitions`. Critically: iRMSD superposes ON the interface backbone atoms themselves and reports the RMSD of those same atoms (no separate reference frame); LRMSD superposes on the FULL receptor backbone and reports RMSD of the FULL ligand backbone with no re-superposition (code uses the private `_rms`).

dockq.equation:
DockQ = ( Fnat + 1/(1 + (LRMSD/d1)^2) + 1/(1 + (iRMSD/d2)^2) ) / 3 ,  with d1 = 8.5 Å (scales LRMSD) and d2 = 1.5 Å (scales iRMSD)

As published, in two pieces.

PLoS ONE 2016, Eq (1), section "Transforming LRMS and iRMS":
  RMS_scaled(RMS, d_i) = 1 / (1 + (RMS/d_i)^2)
  "...d_i is a scaling factor, d1 for LRMS and d2 for iRMS, optimized to d1 = 8.5Å and d2 = 1.5Å"

PLoS ONE 2016, Eq (2), section "Results and Discussion":
  DockQ(Fnat, LRMS, iRMS, d1, d2) = ( Fnat + RMS_scaled(LRMS, d1) + RMS_scaled(iRMS, d2) ) / 3

Bioinformatics 2024 (DockQ v2), Eq (1) — same function, renamed constants:
  DockQ = (1/3) ( f_nat + 1/(1 + (iRMSD/a)^2) + 1/(1 + (LRMSD/b)^2) ),  a = 1.5, b = 8.5

Reference implementation, DockQ.py lines 429-434, VERBATIM:
    def dockq_formula(fnat, irms, lrms):
        return (
            float(fnat)
            + 1 / (1 + (irms / 1.5) * (irms / 1.5))
            + 1 / (1 + (lrms / 8.5) * (lrms / 8.5))
        ) / 3

All three agree exactly. Every term is positive and additive; there is no negative term anywhere in DockQ, and no free intercept. Range is [0, 1]; DockQ = 1 iff Fnat = 1 and both RMSDs = 0 (verified numerically this session).

Optional variant: `--optDockQF1` substitutes the F1 score for fnat in the numerator, where f1(tp, fp, p) = 2*tp/(tp + fp + p) with tp = shared contacts, fp = non-native contacts in the model, p = total native contacts (DockQ.py:425-426, :398). This is a CLI option for mapping optimization / reporting, NOT the definition of DockQ.

dockq.definitions:
OPERATIONAL DEFINITIONS — everything needed to reimplement, transcribed from the fetched sources.

=== 0. ATOM PRE-FILTER (applies to everything downstream) ===
Hydrogens are dropped at PARSE time, in both parsers, before any distance is computed. parsers.py mmCIF path lines 124-126: `element = element_list[i].upper() if element_list else None` / `if element == "H": continue`. parsers.py PDB path lines 351-353: `element = line[76:78].strip().upper()` / `if element == "H": continue`. So "heavy atoms" in the paper is implemented as "all parsed atoms", because H never enters the structure object. Altlocs are de-duplicated by atom id when counting atoms per residue (DockQ.py `list_atoms_per_residue`: `set([a.id for a in residue.get_unpacked_list()])`). HETATM records are skipped unless small-molecule mode is requested.

=== 1. Fnat — fraction of native contacts ===
Paper (PLoS ONE 2016, Introduction), VERBATIM: "the interface between the two interacting protein molecules (receptor and ligand) is defined as any pair of heavy atoms from the two molecules within 5Å of each other. Fnat is then defined as the fraction of native interfacial contacts preserved in the interface of the predicted complex."

Implementation, exactly:
 - Contact unit is a RESIDUE PAIR, not an atom pair. For every cross-chain residue pair (i,j), compute the MINIMUM squared distance over all heavy-atom pairs between residue i and residue j (operations_nocy.py `atom_distances_to_residue_distances`: `res_distances[i,j] = atom_distances[...].min()`). Distances are kept squared throughout and compared against threshold**2 to avoid sqrt.
 - ALL heavy atoms participate — sidechain and backbone alike. This is the one place sidechains matter; iRMSD and LRMSD are backbone-only.
 - Native contact set: residue pairs with min-distance < 5.0 Å (4.0 Å with --capri_peptide).
 - nat_total is computed on the UNTOUCHED native structure before alignment (DockQ.py:285-289, with the source comment "# total number of native contacts is calculated on untouched native structure").
 - Model contact set: same rule applied to the aligned model.
 - Fnat = |native ∩ model| / |native|  (DockQ.py:319 `fnat = nat_total and nat_correct / nat_total or 0`, where nat_correct = `np.sum(model_contacts * native_contacts)`).
 - DENOMINATOR IS THE NATIVE COUNT. See `blockers` — the v2 paper's prose says otherwise and is wrong.
 - Also reported but NOT in the score: fnonnat = non-native model contacts / total model contacts.

=== 2. iRMSD — interface RMSD ===
Paper (PLoS ONE 2016), VERBATIM: "the receptor-ligand interface in the target (native) is redefined at a relatively relaxed atomic contact cutoff of 10Å which is twice the value used to define inter-residue 'interface' contacts in case of Fnat. The backbone atoms of these 'interface' residues is then superposed on their equivalents in the predicted complex (model) to compute the iRMS."

Implementation, exactly (DockQ.py:322-354):
 - Interface residue selection is made ON THE NATIVE/REFERENCE ONLY, never the model. `get_interacting_pairs(ref_res_distances, threshold=interface_threshold**2)` returns the row indices (chain-1 residues) and column indices (chain-2 residues) of every native residue pair within 10 Å.
 - Selection metric: min heavy-atom distance < 10.0 Å. In --capri_peptide mode ONLY, the reference distances are recomputed on CB atoms (CA when the residue has no CB) and thresholded at 8.0 Å.
 - Selected residues from BOTH chains are pooled into one atom set. Duplicates are removed (`residue_subset = set(residue_subset)`).
 - Atoms entering the RMSD: backbone only — N, CA, C, O (plus the nucleic-acid backbone list). Missing atom names are silently skipped via `.index()` in a try block, and model/native are subset in lockstep so the two arrays stay index-matched.
 - Superposition: SVDSuperimposer on those same pooled interface backbone atoms; iRMSD is the RMSD after that optimal superposition. `super_imposer.set(sample_interface_atoms, ref_interface_atoms); super_imposer.run(); irms = super_imposer.get_rms()`. There is NO separate reference frame — iRMSD is superposed on, and measured over, the identical atom set. Whole-complex placement therefore does not affect iRMSD; only interface geometry does.

=== 3. LRMSD — ligand RMSD ===
Paper (PLoS ONE 2016), VERBATIM: "LRMS is the Ligand Root Mean Square deviation calculated for the backbone of the shorter chain (ligand) of the model after superposition of the longer chain (receptor)."

Implementation, exactly (DockQ.py:356-396):
 - Receptor/ligand assignment: receptor = the chain group with MORE residues, ligand = the other; `ligand_chains = (... if ref_group1_size <= ref_group2_size else ...)`, so on an exact tie the FIRST chain group is the receptor. v2 paper sec 2.4: "The receptor is defined as the larger of the two chains by number of amino acids or nucleotides. If two chains are equal in size, the first will be considered the receptor." Size is measured on the REFERENCE, not the model.
 - Superposition set: the FULL receptor backbone (all aligned residues, `subset_atoms(..., atom_types=BACKBONE_ATOMS, what="receptor")` with residue_subset=None -> `range(len(mod_residues))`). NOT interface-restricted.
 - The rotation/translation from that receptor fit is then APPLIED to the model ligand: `rot, tran = super_imposer.get_rotran(); rotated_sample_atoms = np.dot(ligand_atoms_sample, rot) + tran`.
 - RMSD set: the FULL ligand backbone, all aligned residues. Not interface-restricted.
 - No second superposition. The code deliberately calls the private method with the trailing comment "# using the private _rms function which does not superimpose": `lrms = super_imposer._rms(np.asarray(ligand_atoms_native), rotated_sample_atoms)`. LRMSD is therefore a rigid-body placement error in the receptor frame — this is exactly the term that catches "right fold, wrong groove".
 - Small molecules (v2 only): LRMSD is computed over ALL heavy atoms of the ligand (not backbone), superposing on the receptor, i.e. pocket-aligned LRMSD; symmetry-equivalent atom assignments resolved by NetworkX graph matching over covalent-radius edges, taking the lowest LRMSD. No fnat, no iRMSD, and therefore NO DockQ score is emitted for small molecules.

=== 4. RESIDUE CORRESPONDENCE ===
Model-to-native residue equivalence is established by Biopython global sequence alignment per chain (match 5 / mismatch 0 / gap open -4 / gap extend -0.5), or by residue numbering with --no_align. `--allowed_mismatches` controls tolerance when matching a model chain to a native chain. Only aligned residue pairs enter any metric.

=== 5. CAPRI QUALITY BANDS ===
CAPRI class definition, VERBATIM from PLoS ONE 2016 (Introduction, citing ref [10]) — note the mixed AND/OR structure, which is not a simple threshold ladder:
  Incorrect:  Fnat < 0.1  OR  (LRMS > 10 AND iRMS > 4.0)
  Acceptable: ((Fnat >= 0.1 AND Fnat < 0.3) AND (LRMS <= 10.0 OR iRMS <= 4.0))  OR  (Fnat >= 0.3 AND LRMS > 5.0 AND iRMS > 2.0)
  Medium:     ((Fnat >= 0.3 AND Fnat < 0.5) AND (LRMS <= 5.0 OR iRMS <= 2.0))  OR  (Fnat >= 0.5 AND LRMS > 1.0 AND iRMS > 1.0)
  High:       Fnat >= 0.5 AND (LRMS <= 1.0 OR iRMS <= 1.0)
(There is no table in the 2016 paper; I extracted every table-wrap element from the XML and the paper contains none. These criteria are stated in running prose in the Introduction.)

DockQ ranges, VERBATIM from DockQ.py:1078-1081 and README.md:40-43:
  0.00 <= DockQ <  0.23  - Incorrect
  0.23 <= DockQ <  0.49  - Acceptable quality
  0.49 <= DockQ <  0.80  - Medium quality
          DockQ >= 0.80  - High quality
Provenance of those three numbers, VERBATIM from PLoS ONE 2016 Results: "The maximum average F1-score (0.91) was obtained for d1 = 8.5Å and d2 = 1.5Å (Figure B in S1 File), corresponding to the cutoffs C1 = 0.23, C2 = 0.49, and C3 = 0.80 (Fig 1A)." They were fitted jointly with d1/d2, not imposed.

Optimization procedure, VERBATIM: "The two parameters in the DockQ score, d1 and d2, were optimized in a grid search on the MOAL-set by calculating Eq 2 for all pairs of d1 and d2 in the range 0.5 to 10Å for d1, and 0.5 to 5Å for d2 in steps of 0.5." Cutoffs C1/C2/C3 were chosen to maximize MCC between adjacent classes, then the average F1 across the four classes selected (d1, d2).

Numerical self-check run this session with the transcribed formula: DockQ(1, 0, 0) = 1.000; DockQ(0.5, 1.0, 1.0) = 0.726 (High-boundary inputs, sits above C2, below C3); DockQ(0.5, 2.0, 5.0) = 0.534 (Medium band); DockQ(0.3, 4.0, 10.0) = 0.281 (Acceptable band); DockQ(0.05, 8, 20) = 0.079 (Incorrect band). Consistent with the published cutoffs.

=== 6. POSITIVE CONTROL FOR A PEPTIDE-IN-GROOVE PIPELINE ===
RETRIEVED, and this part is short because the sources are short. Neither DockQ paper, nor the reference implementation, nor its README prescribes a positive-control protocol or a redocking target value. There is no sentence anywhere in the fetched material of the form "a redocked complex should score at least X". I am NOT going to invent one.

What IS retrievable and load-bearing for constructing that control:
 (a) The only sanctioned "can it dock at all" line is the Acceptable cutoff: DockQ >= 0.23. Below 0.23 the model is Incorrect by the authors' own calibrated classification. A pipeline that cannot clear 0.23 on a complex whose answer it was handed has not placed the peptide in the groove.
 (b) DockQ = 1.0 exactly iff Fnat = 1 and iRMSD = LRMSD = 0, i.e. iff the model IS the native. Verified numerically. So a bound-bound redock (native receptor conformation, native peptide conformation, only the rigid placement re-derived) has no conformational excuse and its ceiling is 1.0.
 (c) CRITICAL CAVEAT, VERBATIM from the reference implementation's own CLI help (DockQ.py:43-48 and README.md:197): "--capri_peptide  use version for capri_peptide (DockQ cannot not be trusted for this setting)". The double negative is a typo in the source; from context and from the flag's purpose the authors are warning that DockQ is NOT trustworthy in peptide mode. This is the authors flagging their own peptide variant as unreliable. Any peptide-groove benchmark that reports DockQ under --capri_peptide must carry this caveat, and should report raw Fnat / iRMSD / LRMSD alongside the composite rather than relying on the single number.
 (d) The 2016 test-set construction contains a directly transferable positive-control lesson: two CAPRI targets were REMOVED because of "multiple correct chain packings, i.e. same sequence binding at two different locations" (Target37: 2W83, Target40: 3E8L). A peptide that can occupy more than one groove is exactly this failure mode, and a positive control must either pin the mapping with --mapping or accept the best-mapping argmax.

Everything beyond (a)-(d) — e.g. "use DockQ >= 0.80 as the bound-bound redock pass mark" — would be my engineering judgement, not retrieval. Stated as such in `blockers`, not smuggled in here.

The task premise ("GetBestRMS versus AlignMol") encodes the wrong dichotomy, and the paper's own
Methods text is inconsistent with its shipped code. For docking you want NEITHER GetBestRMS nor AlignMol.

  - Paper §2.3 "Quality of fit" states verbatim: PoseBusters "calculates the minimum heavy-atom
    symmetry-aware root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) ... using the RDKit's GetBestRMS function."
  - The CODE has never done that. modules/rmsd.py::_rmsd dispatches on a `kabsch` flag:
        if kabsch is True:  return GetBestRMS(...)
        return CalcRMS(...)
    and check_rmsd calls robust_rmsd with kabsch defaulting to False for the gating value.
    `rmsd_within_threshold = rmsd <= rmsd_threshold` is computed from CalcRMS. GetBestRMS is
    computed too but only reported as the separate diagnostic column `kabsch_rmsd`.
  - I verified this is true at the paper-era commits as well, not just in 0.6.5: the initial
    commit fbe5a34ee (2023-06-02, before the 2023-08-10 submission) already has the identical
    kabsch-flag dispatch with CalcRMS as default.
  - Verified live (posebusters.modules.rmsd.check_rmsd, pose translated 3.0 A):
        rmsd = 3.0   kabsch_rmsd = 0.0   rmsd_within_threshold = False
    GetBestRMS rigidly re-superimposes the pose and returns 0.0, i.e. it would have scored a
    3 A-displaced pose as perfect. CalcRMS correctly fails it.

So: use rdMolAlign.CalcRMS. Using GetBestRMS does not "inflate" RMSD — it DEFLATES it, and would
silently inflate your apparent success rate by scoring poses in the wrong place as correct.
AlignMol is the one that is not symmetry-corrected at all.
posebusters.equation:
SYMMETRY-CORRECTED LIGAND RMSD (the quantity thresholded at 2 A)

  RMSD_symm(P, T) = min over sigma in Aut(G)  sqrt( (1/N) * SUM_{i=1..N} || x^P_{sigma(i)} - x^T_i ||^2 )

  computed IN PLACE — no rotation or translation is fitted between P and T.

where
  T = true (crystal) ligand, P = predicted pose, both heavy atoms only (N heavy atoms),
  Aut(G) = the set of automorphisms of the ligand molecular graph G (element- and bond-order-
           respecting self-mappings), enumerated in RDKit as the substructure matches of the
           molecule onto itself,
  x^P, x^T = Cartesian coordinates in the SAME laboratory frame (the crystal frame).

RDKit call that implements it exactly:
  from rdkit.Chem.rdMolAlign import CalcRMS
  CalcRMS(prbMol=pred, refMol=true, prbId=-1, refId=-1,
          symmetrizeConjugatedTerminalGroups=True, maxMatches=1000000)

CONTRAST OF THE THREE RDKit FUNCTIONS (docstrings read this session from RDKit 2026.03.5):

  CalcRMS     — symmetry-corrected, NO superposition. Docstring: "In contrast to getBestRMS, the
                RMS is computed 'in place', i.e. probe molecules are not aligned to the reference
                ahead of the RMS calculation. This is useful, for example, to compute the RMSD
                between docking poses and the co-crystallized ligand."  <-- THE CORRECT ONE.
  GetBestRMS  — symmetry-corrected AND minimises over rigid-body superposition (Kabsch); "As a
                side-effect, the probe molecule is left in the aligned state." Correct for
                comparing CONFORMERS; wrong for docking, because it discards the binding-site
                placement you are trying to evaluate.
  AlignMol    — NOT symmetry-corrected. Takes a single atom map (first substructure match if none
                supplied), applies a rigid-body fit, returns the resulting RMSD. Wrong on both
                counts for docking.

EMPIRICAL DEMONSTRATION (run this session; p-nitrophenol, |Aut(G)| = 2, non-identity
automorphism (0,1,6,5,4,3,2,7,8,9); pred = identical point cloud with atom labels permuted by
that automorphism, i.e. physically the SAME pose):

  naive index-wise in-place RMSD (no symmetry) : 1.5375 A   <-- inflated; pose looks wrong
  CalcRMS    (symmetry-corrected, in place)    : 0.0000 A   <-- correct
  GetBestRMS (symmetry + re-superposition)     : 0.0000 A
  AlignMol   (single match + superposition)    : 0.9815 A   <-- wrong

And on a genuinely wrong pose (rigidly translated 3.0 A):
  CalcRMS    : 3.0000 A  -> correctly FAILS the 2 A criterion
  GetBestRMS : 0.0000 A  -> wrongly PASSES

Both failure directions are real. Skipping symmetry correction inflates RMSD for symmetric
ligands (1.54 A of pure artefact here, enough to flip a 2 A call). Re-superimposing with
GetBestRMS erases genuine placement error entirely.

--- HOW EACH COUNT IS MADE ---
Bonds: every 1,2 heavy-atom pair from mol.GetBonds(). Angles: every 1,3 pair derived from bond
pairs sharing exactly one atom, scored as the 1-3 DISTANCE (not degrees). Clash pairs: all
remaining heavy-atom pairs (neither 1,2 nor 1,3). A category passes iff number_valid == number
checked, i.e. ZERO violations tolerated once the per-measurement tolerance is applied.
Flatness: SMARTS substructure matches; per-group max distance to the SVD best-fit plane; the
test passes iff ALL matched groups pass; if no group matches, the test passes vacuously.
Conjugated terminal bonds (carboxylate/nitro-like, SMARTS
'[O,N;D1;$([O,N;D1]-[*]=[O,N;D1]),$([O,N;D1]=[*]-[O,N;D1])]~[*]') have their DG bounds
symmetrised before the bond check, so the two C-O bonds of a carboxylate share one bound.

--- RMSD DETAILS ---
heavy_only=True. If mol_true holds several conformers/ligands, RMSD is computed against each and
the MINIMUM is taken (choose_by='rmsd'). robust_rmsd retries on failure in this order:
plain CalcRMS -> uncharged+H-stripped -> neutralised -> canonical tautomer -> neutralised
canonical tautomer -> AssignBondOrdersFromTemplate; returns NaN if all fail. This robustness
ladder exists because docked SDFs routinely disagree with the crystal ligand on protonation and
tautomer, and a naive CalcRMS would just raise and lose the datapoint.

(1) flatness.py::_get_distances_to_plane returns SIGNED projections onto the plane normal, and
    check_flatness takes .max() — not .max() of the absolute value. Confirmed with a
    deliberately asymmetric puckered ring: signed distances
    [0.403, -0.044, -0.268, -0.045, 0.402, -0.448] give .max() = 0.403 whereas |.|max() =
    0.448. So the 0.25 A threshold is applied to the largest POSITIVE excursion and the
    reported max_distance under-states the true worst deviation. Verdicts agree in most cases
    but can differ near the boundary. If you reimplement, decide deliberately which you want.
(2) redock.yml declares the "Energy ratio" module TWICE (lines 128-132 and 133-141). The first
    copy has no chosen_binary_test_output, so it contributes no column — but it does run,
    duplicating the 50-conformer ETKDG+UFF ensemble work. Harmless to correctness, wasteful in
    runtime, and it means the module count in the YAML is one higher than the column count.

  - Paper's summary: DiffDock appears best on RMSD alone, but "when taking physical
    plausibility into account, Gold and AutoDock Vina perform best."

POSEBUSTERS BENCHMARK SET (308 complexes, all released 2021 onwards, i.e. after the training
cut-offs of all five DL methods):
  - AutoDock Vina 58%, Gold 55% — best of the seven methods, both with and without PB-validity.
  - Best DL method DiffDock: 12%.
  - Uni-Mol: 22% on RMSD alone, but "struggles to predict planar aromatic rings and correct
    bond lengths."
  - "EquiBind, Uni-Mol and TankBind generate almost no physically valid poses that pass all tests."
  NOTE ON PRECISION: the sentence "Gold (55%) and AutoDock Vina (58%) perform the best out of
  the seven methods with (solid coral bars) and without (striped coral bars) considering
  PB-validity" is genuinely ambiguous in the source text as to which of the two bar types each
  percentage refers to. The exact per-bar split is encoded in Fig. 1, which I did not obtain as
  data. Treat 55%/58% as "the classical-docking success rate on the Benchmark set" and read
  Fig. 1 / ESI Fig. S6 before quoting either figure as specifically PB-valid or specifically
  RMSD-only.

THE GENERALISATION FINDING (this is the part your receptor-disjoint split should cite):
Paper Results 3.2, Fig. 4. Test cases are stratified by the target receptor's MAXIMUM sequence
identity to any protein in the PDBbind 2020 General Set (the training corpus of all five DL
methods), binned low [0,30%], medium [30%,90%], high [90%,100%].

  - "Without considering physical plausibility (striped bars), the classical methods appear to
    perform as well on the three protein similarity bins while the DL-based methods perform
    worse on the proteins with lower sequence identity. This suggests that the DL-based methods
    are overfitting to the protein targets in their training sets."
  - Conclusion, verbatim: "Our analysis of the targets with sequence identity lower than 30% to
    any member of PDBbind General Set v2020 revealed that across all of the DL-based docking
    methods almost no physically valid poses were generated within the 2 A threshold."
  - The methodological recommendation you should cite for a receptor-disjoint split: "The most
    commonly-used train-test approach for building DL-based docking models is time-based, e.g.,
    complexes released before a certain date are used for training and complexes released later
    for testing. Based on our results, we argue that this is insufficient for testing
    generalisation to novel targets and the sequence identity between the proteins in the
    training and test must be reported on."

So the real result is NOT "DL methods fail on novel sequences by X%". It is a stratified,
largely qualitative claim backed by a figure: classical docking is flat across sequence-identity
bins, DL degrades monotonically as identity drops, and below 30% identity DL produces almost no
poses that are simultaneously physically valid and within 2 A. Do not invent a single headline
percentage for the <30% bin — the paper does not state one in the text.

HOW THE SEQUENCE IDENTITY IS DEFINED (needed to reproduce the split, Methods 2.4):
  identity = (number of exact residue matches after alignment) / (number of residues of the
  QUERY sequence) — note the denominator is the query length, not the alignment length.
  Alignment: Smith-Waterman as implemented in Biopython, BLOSUM62, open gap score -11,
  extension gap score -1. Unknown residues count as mismatches. The stratification value is the
  MAXIMUM identity between ALL chains of the test protein and ALL chains in PDBbind General
  Set v2020.
posebusters.accuracy_dataset:
Two benchmark sets, both defined in the paper (Methods 2.6 / Results):

1. Astex Diverse Set — 85 protein-ligand crystal complexes. Established, widely used, and
   substantially represented in the DL methods' training data, which is precisely why the
   RMSD-vs-PB-valid gap is so wide on it.

2. PoseBusters Benchmark Set — 308 protein-ligand crystal complexes released from 2021 onwards,
   constructed so that no complex is in the training data of any of the seven evaluated methods.
   This is the receptor-generalisation set and the one relevant to your split. It is
   redistributed with the package (posebusters.datasets) and hosted at
   https://zenodo.org/records/8278563 — I did NOT fetch or verify that Zenodo record this
   session, so confirm the DOI/version before you depend on it.

Protocol: cognate re-docking — each ligand is docked back into its own receptor crystal
structure. Search spaces per method are in the paper's Table 3 (Gold: 25 A radius sphere on the
crystal ligand heavy-atom centroid; Vina: 25 A cube on the same centroid; DiffDock: entire
crystal protein; etc.).

Methods evaluated (7): AutoDock Vina, CCDC Gold (classical); DeepDock, DiffDock, EquiBind,
TankBind, Uni-Mol (deep learning). Each also assessed with an optional post-prediction energy
minimisation (AMBER ff14SB protein + OpenFF Sage ligand in OpenMM, protein atoms fixed,
converged to 0.01 kJ/mol).

Threshold provenance worth knowing, because it tells you these are calibrated floors and not
arbitrary round numbers: the paper states the 25%/30% geometry tolerances were chosen because
"all but one of the crystal ligands in the Astex Diverse set and all of those in the PoseBusters
Benchmark set pass at this threshold"; the 0.25 A flatness threshold "admits all Astex Diverse
and PoseBusters Benchmark set crystal structures by a wide margin"; the 0.75 distance cutoff
passes all Astex and all but one Benchmark crystal structure; and the energy ratio of 100 (vs
Wills et al.'s stricter 7) rejects "only one structure each" from the two sets. In other words
the suite is deliberately tuned so that real crystal structures pass — it is a floor for gross
implausibility, not a measure of pose quality.

The additions are all post-publication: minimum distance to waters, volume overlap with waters, non-aromatic ring NON-flatness (>= 0.05 A, an inverted test), no_radicals, inchi_convertible, and all_atoms_connected. If you report a 'PB-valid' rate you MUST state the package version, because PB-validity is strictly harder in 0.6.5 than in the paper and the numbers are not comparable across versions. FIG. 1 AND FIG. 4 UNDERLYING NUMBERS NOT RETRIEVED. The <30%-identity generalisation result is stated in the text qualitatively ('almost no physically valid poses were generated within the 2 A threshold') and I have quoted it verbatim rather than inventing a percentage. Retrieve the ESI from https://doi.org/10.1039/d3sc04185a before quoting any specific number for the low-identity bin.

RECEPTOR-DISJOINT SPLIT — REPRODUCE THE PAPER'S DEFINITION EXACTLY OR YOUR SPLIT IS NOT COMPARABLE. Identity = exact residue matches / length of the QUERY sequence (denominator is query length, NOT alignment length), via Smith-Waterman in Biopython with BLOSUM62, open gap -11, extend gap -1, unknown residues counted as mismatches, taking the MAXIMUM over all chain-vs-all-chain comparisons against the training corpus. Bins: low [0,30%], medium [30%,90%], high [90%,100%]. Note this identity measure is asymmetric because of the query-length denominator, so fix which side is the query.

RECEPTOR FILE FORMAT IS A CORRECTNESS DEPENDENCY, NOT A CONVENIENCE. tools/protein.py partitions the receptor into protein / organic cofactor / inorganic cofactor / water using PDB HETATM flags and CCD residue names. If an atom has no PDBResidueInfo the code assumes it is organic and merely logs a warning. Feeding a receptor that has lost residue names or hetero flags will silently misroute atoms into the wrong test with the wrong radii type (covalent vs vdW) and the wrong vdW scale (0.5 vs 0.8), producing plausible-looking but wrong verdicts. Load receptors from PDB with proximityBonding=False, sanitize=False, as the shipped loading config does.

MINOR IMPLEMENTATION QUIRK, VERIFIED, WORTH KNOWING IF YOU REIMPLEMENT: flatness.py takes .max() of the SIGNED distances to the best-fit plane rather than the max absolute deviation. Confirmed on a constructed asymmetric pucker where signed .max() = 0.403 A but |.|max() = 0.448 A. The 0.25 A threshold is therefore applied to the largest positive excursion, and the reported max_distance under-states the worst deviation. Rarely changes a verdict, but it means a reimplementation using abs() will not reproduce PoseBusters bit-for-bit near the boundary.

PERFORMANCE, NOT CORRECTNESS: redock.yml declares the Energy ratio module twice (lines 128-132 and 133-141); the first declaration produces no output column but still runs the full 50-conformer ETKDGv3 + UFF ensemble, roughly doubling the cost of the most expensive check. get_energies is @cache'd on the InChI string, which mitigates this within a run but not across processes. Budget accordingly for a 308-complex sweep.

CONFIGURABILITY CAVEAT FOR REPORTING: every threshold in this suite is user-adjustable via the YAML, and the paper repeatedly stresses this. A bare claim of 'PB-valid' is therefore under-specified. Report the package version and the config name ('redock' vs 'dock' vs 'mol' vs the *_fast variants), and archive the actual YAML you ran with alongside your results.

errors.item: Receptor/ligand assignment on an exact size tie
errors.claimed: Report states: 'on an exact tie the FIRST chain group is the receptor', and presents the code as implementing the v2 paper sentence 'If two chains are equal in size, the first will be considered the receptor' — i.e. code and paper agree.

On a tie, `g1 > g2` is False so receptor = SECOND group, and `g1 <= g2` is True so ligand = FIRST group. Confirmed decisively by the authors' own README module example (README.md ~line 235), which shows for an equal-size pair: 'len1': 124, 'len2': 124, 'class1': 'ligand', 'class2': 'receptor' — chain1 (first) is the ligand. Consequently the v2 paper (Bioinformatics 2024, sec 2.4) CONTRADICTS its own reference implementation on this point — a second code-vs-prose discrepancy of exactly the kind the report was tasked to find, which it missed and instead reported as agreement. Materially affects LRMSD (hence DockQ) only for equal-size chain pairs, since LRMSD is asymmetric under receptor/ligand swap; negligible for peptide-in-groove where sizes differ greatly.

Threshold-calibration provenance confirmed verbatim from the paper, and it matters for how you report results: "The tolerance used throughout this manuscript is 25% for bond lengths and bond angles and 30% for non-covalently bound pairs of atoms... This was selected as all but one of the crystal ligands in the Astex Diverse set and all of those in the PoseBusters Benchmark set pass at this threshold." The suite is deliberately tuned so real crystal structures pass — it is a floor for gross implausibility, not a measure of pose quality, exactly as the submission frames it.

Benchmark results confirmed verbatim from Europe PMC. Astex Diverse Set: "For the 85 test cases in the Astex Diverse set 50 (59%) predictions have RMSD within 2 A RMSD and 5 (5.9%) pass all tests" (TankBind) — the ~10x gap is real. PoseBusters Benchmark: "Gold (55%) and AutoDock Vina (58%) perform the best out of the seven methods with (solid coral bars) and without (striped coral bars) considering PB-validity" — the submission's warning that this sentence is genuinely ambiguous as to which bar each percentage denotes is correct and I confirm it from the source text.

The generalisation finding is correctly characterised as qualitative, not a headline percentage. Conclusion sentence confirmed verbatim: "across all of the DL-based docking methods almost no physically valid poses were generated within the 2 A threshold" (for targets with sequence identity lower than 30% to any member of PDBbind General Set v2020). The submission's refusal to invent a percentage for the <30% bin is the correct call.

Sequence-identity definition for a receptor-disjoint split, confirmed verbatim: "sequence identity between two amino acid chains is the number of exact residue matches after sequence alignment divided by the number of residues of the query sequence. The sequence alignment used is the Smith-Waterman algorithm implemented in Biopython using an open gap score of -11 and an extension gap score of -1 and the BLOSUM62 substitution matrix." The query-length denominator makes the measure asymmetric, so fix which side is the query — the submission's warning is correct.

Version-skew warning is correct and important. posebusters 0.6.5 emits 25 checks; the paper's Table 4 describes 19. PB-validity is strictly harder in 0.6.5 than in the paper, so any reported PB-valid rate MUST state the package version and config name. Pin the version.

Top-line recommendation stands: do not reimplement. `pip install posebusters` (MIT) and call it. The thresholds are only half the story — the atom-classification logic in tools/protein.py and the robust_rmsd fallback ladder (plain CalcRMS -> uncharged+H-stripped -> neutralised -> canonical tautomer -> neutralised canonical tautomer -> AssignBondOrdersFromTemplate -> NaN, all verified in modules/rmsd.py) are where a reimplementation would silently diverge.
